blocks.c: You walk the floors at eleven, one, three and five. You check thirty-one landings, two basements, four risers and the roof. You log what you find. If the log says something is broken, day shift fixes it. If the log says nothing, day shift assumes nothing happened, and day shift is wrong about that roughly twice a week.

I have done it for fourteen months. I am twenty-four. I took it because it pays a little over what a warehouse pays and because nobody talks to me, which at the time I thought was the best part of it.

The Merridew Tower is not haunted. I want that on the record early, because of what comes later. It is a 1974 office building with an aluminium curtain wall, a chiller that howls in August, and a smell in the north stair that nobody has ever identified. Thirty-one floors. Two basements. Six tenants, of whom four are law firms, which tells you everything.
There are two elevators for people and one freight car at the back.
The freight car is the oldest thing in the building. Original 1974 cab, replaced motor, replaced governor, original panel: a brass plate with round buttons worn concave by fifty years of thumbs.
The buttons go 31 down to 1, then B1, then B2. Written out, the plate looks like this, and I have drawn it in the log book four times now for four different people who did not believe me:
Under B2, at the bottom of the plate, there is a keyhole.

I asked about the keyhole in my first week. My supervisor, Mrs. Dalisay, said it was for the fire service and that the key was lost in the nineties, and she said it in the flat, finished voice that people use when a conversation is over.
I believed her for fourteen months.
Then, on a Tuesday in March, at 3:14 in the morning, on a floor walk I had done four hundred times, I found a key taped to the underside of the fire extinguisher bracket on B2.
It was small. It was brass. It had a paper tag.
The tag said, in handwriting I did not recognise: SORRY.
